paras: The killing of Albert Dennis was the fatal shooting of a young Black man by Milan E. McNamara, a special policeman employed by the Great Northern theater in Chicago, outside the theater on the evening of Sunday, November 29, 1903. Dennis had just been ejected from the theater, and he died a short time later at the county hospital. White papers carried the shooting as a brief wire item, while the Chicago Broad Ax reported that Dennis's Knights of Pythias lodge had voted to pay for McNamara's prosecution.

According to the Chicago Broad Ax, Dennis was a young man who had belonged to Hannibal Lodge No. 6, Knights of Pythias, for seven months, and his former home was Knoxville, Tennessee, where his father, George Dennis, lived. The wire reports gave his address as 3138 La Salle street but identified him only provisionally, as a man "believed to be" or "supposed to be" Albert Dennis. McNamara appeared in the dispatches as a special policeman of the theater and in the Broad Ax as "the private watchman at the Great Northern Theater."

The shooting took place on Sunday evening, just before the beginning of the performance, after Dennis had been put out of the theater. A Chicago dispatch dated November 30 said it occurred in front of the theater building "after a fight between the colored man, the special policeman and several others." A second version of the dispatch, datelined December 1, placed it on the sidewalk before "hundreds of patrons" and said Dennis had been ejected for a disturbance he was "said to have caused." The Broad Ax located the shooting at the Quincy street entrance to the theater.
Dennis was struck in the forehead and taken to the county hospital, where he lived only a short time.

The wire reports said McNamara was locked up after the shooting. On December 8, Hannibal Lodge, which the Broad Ax called the largest lodge in Illinois, voted unanimously to pay the expense of prosecuting McNamara. It appointed a committee of five members to work with its chancellor commander, the lawyer Albert B. George, in gathering evidence and taking steps to bring McNamara "to trial and punishment."

The lodge also voted the usual funeral expenses, and Dennis's body was sent to Knoxville, where Toussaint L'Ouverture Lodge conducted the services. No report of an inquest, grand jury action or trial of McNamara appears in the coverage.

In the white press the killing reached readers only as a short Chicago wire item, printed between November 30 and December 5 in the Beatrice Daily Express, the Waterbury Evening Democrat and the Gilpin Observer. The Wisconsin Tobacco Reporter, the Jasper Weekly Courier and the Osceola Times carried versions of the same dispatch. Most headlines were flat, such as "Killed by Special Policeman" and "Killed in a Theater Crowd," though the Waterbury paper's subhead read "Colored Man Got Into a Row and Was Shot." The dispatches called the dead man a "colored man" or "negro," named him only tentatively, and gave the fight and the disturbance with no account from his side.

The Chicago Broad Ax printed the lodge's report on its front page on December 12, signed "W." It described Dennis as "a young man of quiet and peaceful habits," held that McNamara had shot him "without any just provocation," and declared that such outrages called for "action, and not resolutions and speeches," in the name of the order and the race.

The accounts differ on what led to the shooting. The unsourced wire reports said Dennis had caused a disturbance in the theater and fought with the special policeman and several others before he was shot. The lodge's statement said his death followed "a misunderstanding about his seats," that three theater employes had ejected him, and that he was unarmed, in the street and "but a boy in appearance" when McNamara fired. The two presses also name him differently, as Albert Dennis in the wire and as R. Elbert Dennis in the Broad Ax.

reader.title: Killing of Albert Dennis
bases: A special policeman employed by the theater shot and killed a Black man he had helped eject (A1, A4), described by the Broad Ax as the theater's 'private watchman' (A7); no mob or crowd took part in the killing.

The white wire (A1, A4) and the Chicago Broad Ax's report of the lodge's action (A7, A8) independently agree that McNamara of the Great Northern theater shot and killed Dennis after his ejection on Sunday evening, Nov. 29.
